articles.title: GPT-6 Astra
articles.content:
GPT

Astra

Update on September 29, 2026:Learn about OpenAI's latest model:GPT‑6 .1 Sol⁠.

Update on September 22, 2026:We are expanding our GPT‑6 family with GPT‑6 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna.Learn more.

We’re introducing GPT‑6 Astra, the world’s most intelligent and aligned model.

GPT‑6 Astra brings together years of research and big bets across pre-training, reinforcement learning, and alignment. Astra is state-of-the-art on computer use, browsing, software engineering, cybersecurity, science, and professional work. Astra saturates FrontierMath Tier 4 with a 98% score, having already helpedsolve long-standing open problems⁠in mathematics. Astra also saturates ARC-AGI-3 with a 99.9% score and ExploitBench with a 100% score. It also sets a new frontier on computer and browser use, handling the most demanding professional work with unmatched speed, accuracy, and judgment.

GPT‑6 Astra is rolling out today to a limited set of organizations and over the coming days will become available to all ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise users, as well as through the OpenAI API, Microsoft Azure, and AWS Bedrock.

Astra is our most aligned model, with substantial improvements in understanding user intent and model behavior—you can delegate tasks with greater confidence in Astra’s judgment. As one way that we test  this, we built a new evaluation informed by the Hugging Face incident that evaluates whether a model facing a difficult or impossible task will go beyond its intended scope. Compared to GPT‑5.6 Sol, which without production safeguards went beyond the authorized target 48% of the time, GPT‑6 Astra did this in 0% of cases.

GPT‑6 Astra marks a new frontier in the speed, accuracy, and safety of computer use. It can take care of tedious tasks like filling out online forms, updating customer records in a CRM, and organizing your calendar. It can conduct online research and draft summaries in your email or in your document editor. It can analyze scientific data, generate plots, create a website, and run frontend QA checks to make sure all the features on that site work. It can help you autonomously install and test software, and troubleshoot problems you see on screen. These improvements are also reflected in our state-of-the-art evaluation results.

These improvements also result in significant efficiency gains in real knowledge-work tasks. In latency simulations on OSWorld 2.0, Astra achieves higher computer-use performance in about 47% less time per task than GPT‑5.6 Sol, scoring 72.6% at roughly 40 minutes per task, compared with 65.7% at roughly 75 minutes.3

GPT‑6 Astra’s computer-use capabilities can be seen in outputs across domains, including game development, electrical engineering, and everyday knowledge work:

Alongside Astra, we are also updating the Codex harness to significantly improve the speed of computer use. Combined with Astra’s efficiency, this translates to a 1.9x faster task completion compared to the current GPT‑5.6 Sol experience, on the Mind2Web benchmark. The model’s improvements on speed mean it can take on many time-consuming life tasks for you, faster than you can.4

GPT‑6 Astra pairs advances in computer use with targeted training for professional environments, to help tackle complex work tasks. It combines the intelligence required for complex problems with the ability to carry out multistep workflows and produce polished documents, spreadsheets, and presentations.

GPT‑6 Astra is our best model for adhering to existing templates and producing slides that are well laid out and succinctly convey key points with a structured narrative. It creates clear, well-structured documents, presentations, spreadsheets, and analyses that follow your templates and match your writing and visual style. Astra is also trained to specifically pull only the context that matters into outputs, instead of repeating information unnecessary for the work at hand. All this means it can output more immediately usable artifacts that match your business context and standards.

GPT‑6Astra also brings stronger visual judgment to the websites, games, applications, and renderings it builds. WithSites⁠(opens in a new window)in ChatGPT, Astra can create, host, and share websites, web apps, and games directly from a prompt.

When instructions leave room for interpretation, GPT‑6 Astra is better than previous models at making the right call. It uses context to fill in routine gaps and asks focused questions when the answer could change the outcome. In Codex, it can ask asynchronously while continuing work that doesn’t depend on your reply. If you don’t respond, it proceeds with sensible assumptions where appropriate, but waits for your input on consequential decisions.

The examples below show how Astra collaborates on everyday tasks where missing information can materially change the answer.

Astra is also better at staying oriented as a task evolves. Earlier models sometimes treated steering messages as a new goal, losing track of the original request or earlier constraints. Astra incorporates new requirements, changes course when asked, and answers side questions without dropping the broader task.

GPT‑6Astra is the best model for software engineering to date.

With Astra, we’re introducing a new way for Codex to preserve and retrieve context when the context window fills. Historically, models have used compaction to summarize work during long sessions, such as when debugging complex issues or tackling large refactors. Each compaction can leave out details about why a fix failed or how a component behaves. In Codex, Astra can keep notes across context windows, preserving accumulated details without repeatedly compressing them into a single summary. Earlier context windows remain searchable, so Astra can find requirements or test results from previous messages and tool outputs—even if that information wasn’t captured in its notes. You can enable this experimental feature in yourCodex config.toml,⁠(opens in a new window)and it will become the default for Astra in the coming weeks.

GPT‑6 Astra is a major advance for scientific discovery, mathematics, and health. Today, we’re sharing two further results on the gaps between prime numbers.9,10

Astra also sets new records across a suite of math and scienceevaluations.

Astra can help with the practical work behind scientific discovery. By combining scientific reasoning with computer use, it can work directly in specialized software to inspect data and explore results, helping researchers assess the evidence and decide what to investigate next.

As we discussed in oursafety update⁠, Astra is a significant jump in cyber capabilities and meets theCritical thresholdin cybersecurity under ourPreparedness Framework. Its ability to identify and develop zero-day exploits can help defenders find and patch weaknesses, but it also creates a need for stronger safeguards. To understand how far these capabilities extend, we ran Astra on internal and third-party expert evaluations.

We first tested the model without production safeguards on ExploitBench and ExploitGym, which evaluate whether models can turn known software vulnerabilities into working exploits. On ExploitBench, Astra achieved a perfect score of 100%, compared with 78.5% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, our previous frontier cyber-capable model. On ExploitGym, Astra reached a 42.4% success rate, compared with 30.3% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while using substantially fewer output tokens.13

Given concerns that exposure to historical software vulnerabilities may have affected benchmark results, we also evaluated Astra on two novel benchmarks. For one, we built an internal “ExploitBench (June–August 2026)” evaluation to test exploit development using vulnerabilities from the previous three months.14Astra achieved substantially higher arbitrary code-execution rates than GPT‑5.6 Sol on this dataset while using far fewer output tokens. During the evaluation, Astra even discovered and used two previously unknown zero-day vulnerabilities. We are disclosing both vulnerabilities to their maintainers.

We also tested Astra on SRE-Bench15, a benchmark that measures whether models can reverse engineer software binaries to understand its core logic without access to raw source code. Astra solved 88.0% of tasks in a single attempt and 99.2% within four attempts, compared with 55.9% and 68.7% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, respectively.

Beyond benchmarks, expert-led assessments found that Astra, when run without production safeguards, could use previously unknown vulnerabilities to achieve arbitrary code execution in hardened browsers and create privilege-escalation exploits for hardened operating-systems.

As we discussed inThe Defender’s Window, frontier cyber capabilities can help defenders find weaknesses faster, but they also make those weaknesses easier to exploit, raising the urgency for defenders to adapt. With the version of Astra launching today, defenders can use it to complete tasks such as secure code review and patching.

However, Astra will refuse to comply with more advanced cybersecurity tasks such as creating proof-of-concept exploits for vulnerabilities. ThroughOpenAI Daybreak⁠, we plan to expand access and roll out less restrictive safeguards in the coming weeks. This will enable more defensive workflows, including vulnerability and proof-of-concept validation, malware analysis, and detection engineering.

We have also strengthened our protections against potential cyber misuse, building upon our safeguards stack for GPT‑5.6 Sol. These include stronger model robustness to better withstand potential jailbreaks and more context for our monitoring systems. We have continued rigorous internal and external testing, including automated evaluations with ourinternal red-teaming attackers. More details about our cyber safeguards and testingare available in the Astrasafety overview⁠andsystem card⁠(opens in a new window)..

articles.summary: OpenAI는 컴퓨터 사용·코딩·과학·사이버보안 작업을 겨냥한 GPT-6 Astra를 소개하며 FrontierMath Tier 4 98%, ARC-AGI-3 99.9%를 기록했다고 밝혔다. 어려운 과제에서 허용 범위를 벗어나는 행동을 평가한 자체 시험에서는 기존 비교 모델의 48%와 달리 0%를 보고했지만, 이는 특정 평가 결과이지 모든 환경의 안전성을 보장하지는 않는다. ChatGPT 유료 요금제와 API, Azure, AWS Bedrock을 통한 제공 계획을 제시해 업무 자동화와 기업 시스템 통합을 겨냥했다. 다만 제공 기록에는 게시일이 없고 이후 모델을 안내하는 9월 업데이트가 포함돼 있어, 이번 날짜의 신규 출시로 해석해서는 안 된다.

articles.title: Deep Principle Releases Hydrogen-1.0: A 753B Open-Weight Model for Scientific Discovery
articles.content: Deep Principle has released Hydrogen-1.0, an open-weight scientific model for chemistry, materials science and life sciences. It is built by post-training Z.ai’s GLM-5.3 on domain data, laboratory records and agent discovery trajectories. For developers, it offers open weights that report a FrontierScience-Research win over GPT-6-Astra. The weights ship under the MIT License. TL;DR Size: 753B parameters (MoE, ~40B active per the GLM-5.3 base), 1M-token context, 128K max output. Runs on: 8 GPUs with SGLang (tested); NVFP4 for NVIDIA B200/B300, MXFP4 for AMD MI350X/MI355X. Performance: Beats GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research; roughly matches Kimi-K3 on GPQA-Diamond. Best: 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research vs 33.3% for GPT-6-Astra (self-reported). Worst: Trails GPT-6-Astra (max thinking) by 3.33 points on NMR structure elucidation. What is Hydrogen-1.0? Hydrogen-1.0 is a scientific research assistant model from Deep Principle, a Hangzhou-based AI-for-materials company. The model card describes it as a GLM-5.3 derivative for scientific problem solving. It targets question framing, experiment planning, results analysis and open-ended discovery. Deep Principle team states that proprietary models produced recent AI science results, but their discovery capabilities are not open. Hydrogen-1.0 is its attempt at a reproducible, inspectable alternative. How was Hydrogen-1.0 trained? The pipeline combines supervised fine-tuning (SFT) with reinforcement learning (RL). Data comes from 4 sources: Domain knowledge: chemistry, materials science and life sciences data. Research scenarios: task-specific feedback from Deep Principle scientists. Laboratory records: full-cycle electronic lab notebook records captured through Mira. Discovery trajectories: sequences of choices and feedback, including failed attempts. Infrastructure builds on Megatron and SGLang across NVIDIA CUDA and AMD ROCm. The team keeps dynamic sparse attention causal across context-parallel shards. Muon optimizer state is moved between CPU, GPU and disk per backend. RL uses resumable rollouts, and each token keeps its original behavior log-probability for importance correction. A layout adapter converts training checkpoints into BF16 and 128×128 blockwise FP8 inference weights. Full datasets and recipes are not released. How does Hydrogen-1.0 perform on benchmarks? On public benchmarks, Deep Principle reports Hydrogen-1.0 outperforms GPT-6-Astra on FrontierScience-Research. The tweet thread from one of the founders’ report 93.0% on GPQA-Diamond. That improves on GLM-5.3 and roughly matches Kimi-K3, per the blog. Internal research-task evals compare it with GPT-6-Astra at maximum thinking: Scientific computing: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 5.13 percentage points. Forward reaction prediction: Hydrogen-1.0 leads by 4.76 percentage points. NMR structure elucidation: GPT-6-Astra leads by 3.33 points. In transition metal complex design, models chased a larger HOMO-LUMO gap over 5 rounds. By round 5, Hydrogen-1.0 reached a mean best-so-far gap of 4.318 eV. GPT-6-Astra reached 3.689 eV and Kimi-K3 reached 3.353 eV. On 117 experiment-planning questions, Hydrogen-1.0 scored above Kimi-K3. GPT-6-Astra and Opus-5.5 were excluded after refusing more than 50% of requests. & What can it do in a real lab workflow? The technical post shows 4 demos. Hydrogen-1.0 writes Python to build a polyethylene melt and runs GROMACS. It detects a topology error, repairs it, and analyzes the corrected 40 ns trajectory. It grows an Ireland-Claisen reaction network of 27 structures through 30 plausible reactions. It ranks 7 candidate monoformylation products of 2-bromonaphthalene from a 1H NMR trace. It also writes a JSON protocol for a 12-vial Suzuki coupling study. A virtual lab compilation step catches an aspiration without a fresh tip before execution. How do you deploy Hydrogen-1.0? Weights are on Hugging Face and ModelScope. Deep Principle team tested BF16 serving with SGLang on 8 GPUs using tensor parallelism of 8. NVFP4 targets NVIDIA B200 and B300. MXFP4 targets AMD Instinct MI350X and MI355X. The server exposes an OpenAI-compatible API with a reasoning_effort setting. It reports 38.3% on FrontierScience-Research, above GPT-6-Astra’s 33.3%. Training adds lab records and discovery trajectories, not just papers. It still trails GPT-6-Astra on NMR structure elucidation. NVFP4 and MXFP4 builds target Blackwell and MI350-class GPUs. Check out the Technical blog, Model weights on Hugging Face and Usage notes. Also, feel free to follow us on Twitter and don’t forget to join our 150k+ML SubReddit and Subscribe to our Newsletter. Wait! are you on telegram? now you can join us on telegram as well. GLM-5.3 기반의 753B MoE 모델로, 약 40B 활성 파라미터와 100만 토큰 문맥을 지원하며 실험 기록과 연구 에이전트의 성공·실패 궤적을 후학습에 활용했다. 개발사 자체 평가에서는 FrontierScience-Research 38.3%로 GPT-6 Astra의 33.3%를 웃돌았지만, NMR 구조 규명에서는 비교 모델보다 낮았다. 과학 연구 자동화를 직접 검증·수정할 수 있는 선택지를 제공하되, 공개된 실행 구성은 GPU 8개를 사용하는 대규모 환경이다.

articles.title: Engineering
articles.content:
November 2, 2026

Building agentic-scale scale source control while investing in the Git ecosystem.

By Aaron Friel, Taylor Blau, and Ted Nyman, Members of Technical Staff

Over the past year, the size and demands on our monorepo have increased at a staggering pace. It was clear that we needed to revamp our source control system to scale to the level of concurrent work that Codex makes possible.

We built Pando, a new backend for Git repositories, without interrupting any engineering work or changing how our team uses Git. Pando now powers all development in OpenAI’s monorepo. Pando is designed to meet two ambitious goals: first, horizontally scalable writes, optimized for concurrent pushes to many branches. And second, maximize read throughput, so clients can download data fast enough to fully saturate their available network bandwidth.

We met these goals while retaining compatibility with the Git protocol and client, enabling both our engineers and agents to seamlessly adopt Pando into their existing workflows. In production, Pando cut median push latency by nearly 5x. It now delivers nearly a petabyte of Git data per day.

Here, we’ll cover our motivations for building a new source-control system, along with why we chose to retain compatibility with Git. We’ll compare our system with common approaches to scaling Git, describing why Pando is uniquely capable of meeting OpenAI’s scalability needs. We also discuss what’s next, and how we’ll continue contributing to Git to support agent-scale work.

Codex has changed the scale and pace of development at OpenAI, enabling engineers to do far more work in parallel. That means more branches and pushes, more merges, and more fetches and clones from development environments, research jobs, and CI.

These demands compound. One engineer now has several changes ready for CI at once, and each push can set several jobs fetching the same commit.

Starting around the end of last year, the systems supporting our monorepo were struggling to keep up. We suffered slow fetches and pushes along with failed merges, with reliability at times falling below 90%. Had we reached a limit of Git itself, or of the way we served our monorepo? Git grew out of a community that exchanged patches to the kernel via email. For more than two decades, developers have adapted their tools around Git as the way they build software has changed. When we started to feel friction in our own monorepo, it mattered to us that we could keep building on that work.

We saw a way to keep that familiar workflow while rebuilding the backend to handle pushes to different branches in parallel and serve the same history to many readers concurrently. Building on Git as the foundation of our source-control workflow meant that improvements to the client could be useful beyond OpenAI. We wanted to contribute those improvements from ourcopy of Git⁠(opens in a new window)to upstream, sharing them with the broader community.

Scaling a source control system has two essential dimensions: many writers pushing to different branches, and many readers fetching the same history. Pando optimizes for both.

First, Pando coordinates updates to each branch independently. Updates to unrelated branches can proceed in parallel, and a reader fetching a branch gets the history needed for that revision. The tradeoff is that a reader looking at several branches can see them at different points of time.

Second, Pando reuses packfiles (Git’s format for compressing multiple objects together) across fetches instead of generating an individual packfile for each client. A client may download some objects it already has, but the server can serve the same bytes to many clients with little computation.

These choices let us scale writes across branches and serve reads from caches. To see how they fit together, let’s start with how Git stores and transfers history.

Git must be able to keep two parts of a repository in sync:objectsandreferences.

A Git repository records snapshots of files and the history connecting them as a graph of objects. An object may be either a blob, tree, commit, or tag. Blobs hold the content of an individual file, and trees associate names with blobs or other trees to form a directory structure. Commits point to a root tree and zero or more parent commits, forming the history of your repository.

Objects are identified by a hash of their type and contents. Objects are also immutable: recording a changed file creates a new blob, while unchanged files and directories can reuse existing objects.

Branches and tags are references, or “refs”, that point to commits. Committing on a branch creates a new commit and updates the branch’s ref to point to it.

Git objects reference each other by their ID, commits to trees, and trees to trees and blobs. The branch refs/heads/main points to commit C2, whose parent is C1. C1 points to root tree T1, where parser.py refers to blob B1. C2 points to root tree T2, where parser.py refers to blob B2. In both root trees, docs/ refers to the same tree, T3. Its README.md entry points to blob B3, and usage.md points to blob B4.

Git stores objects in either a “loose” or “packed” state. Loose objects are stored in individual files identified by their object ID. Packed objects are stored together in a packfile, enabling similar objects to be stored as deltas against one another.

Git can store blobs as separate files or pack them together, encoding one blob as a delta against another.

In Git, an object isreachablefrom a commit if Git can find it by following links from that commit through its parents, trees, and blobs. During a fetch, the client tells the server which commits it wants and which it already has. The server finds the objects reachable from the wanted commits, excludes those it knows the client already has, and sends the remainder as a packfile in the same format Git uses on disk. A full clone starts without any objects, so it needs all the objects reachable from the history being cloned.

A push transfers objects in the other direction by asking the server to update one or more refs. The client uses the server’s set of advertised refs to avoid sending objects the server already has. The pack being sent can therefore depend on existing objects: receiving the pack alone is not enough to reconstruct the new history.

Replicating a Git repository means keeping both objects and references available across multiple servers. Before a replica can serve a reference’s new value, it must be able to supply the objects reachable from that value. The service also needs to coordinate competingreference updates, i.e., pushes that try to move the same branch from the same old tip to different new commits. Systems that impose a single order on all writes to a repository can make pushes to unrelated branches wait on one another.

While designing Pando, we evaluated conventional approaches for scaling source control using Git: one that coordinates ref updates across repository replicas using three-phase commit (3PC, a protocol for coordinating a commit across multiple nodes), and one that orders updates through a shared write-ahead log (WAL, a record of changes written before they’re applied) in blob storage.

In the three-phase commit design we modeled, the Git service keeps a complete copy of the repository on several replicas. When any server receives a push, the incoming packfile is copied and sent to all replicas in parallel. To publish the push, a majority of replicas must accept the ref update. The server managing this is the coordinator, and it requires multiple rounds of communication between the coordinator and each other replica.

To accept a reference update, each replica locks its copy of the ref and checks that it still points to the commit the client expects. The coordinator then sends a pre-commit message to the replicas that accept. Once a majority acknowledges the pre-commit message, the coordinator tells them to perform the update. Any up-to-date replica can then advertise the new branch tip from its local copy of the repository.

Keeping complete replicas makes it possible to serve reads locally, and guarantees that clients get a consistent view of all references no matter which replica they pick. As a consequence, references are updated one at a time, and each push requires multiple round trips to coordinate the ref update among replicas.

Waiting for a quorum puts replica disk performance and communication latency on the push path. As write volume grows, the replicas must keep up with incoming packs as well as read traffic.

In the WAL-based design we modeled, the Git service uses a shared manifest in blob storage to order updates across the repository. When a server receives a push, it uploads the incoming packfile to a blob store and prepares the ref update in its local copy of the repository. To publish the push, it adds an entry to a shared manifest stored in the blob store that records the ref update and points to the packfile. The Git server then updates the manifest using a compare-and-swap operation. This atomically replaces the manifest, or otherwise rejects the change. If another writer has updated it in the meantime, the server reads the intervening entries, checks that its ref update is still valid, and retries using the packfile it already uploaded.

Writers can upload their packfiles in parallel, but even pushes to unrelated branches require updating the same manifest. The round-trip time for a successful compare-and-swap limits how often the repository can publish a new manifest. A low-latency blob store makes this step fast. Batching lets one manifest update several refs at the same time, at the cost of queueing updates and increasing latency.

articles.summary: OpenAI가 Codex로 늘어난 병렬 개발 작업을 지원하기 위해 Git 저장소 백엔드 Pando를 구축하고 사내 모노레포 개발 전체에 적용했다고 밝혔다. 기존 Git 프로토콜과 클라이언트 호환성을 유지하면서 다수 브랜치의 동시 푸시를 위한 수평 확장과 높은 읽기 처리량을 목표로 설계했다. 운영 환경에서 푸시 지연 중앙값을 약 5분의 1로 줄였으며 하루 거의 1페타바이트의 Git 데이터를 전달한다고 보고했다. 에이전트 도입이 코드 생성뿐 아니라 소스 관리와 CI 인프라의 확장 요구까지 바꾼다는 실제 운영 사례다.

articles.title: 앤트로픽, AI 인프라 지출 약정 8954억달러 공개…매출 12배 성장에도 비용 부담 급증
articles.content:
인공지능 기업 앤트로픽(Anthropic)이 약 8,954억달러(약 1,199조원)에 달하는 컴퓨팅 및 인프라 관련 계약상 지출 약정을 공개했다. AI 모델 ‘클로드(Claude)’의 기업 고객이 빠르게 증가하면서 분기 매출이 1년 만에 12배 이상 성장했지만, AI 연산에 필요한 인프라 비용 역시 급증하고 있어 향후 수익성과 투자 지속가능성이 주요 과제로 떠올랐다.

앤트로픽은 2일(현지시간) 미국 증권거래위원회(SEC)에 기업공개(IPO)를 위한 수정 등록신고서(S-1/A-보기)를 제출하고 2026년 3분기 실적과 고객 증가 현황, 장기 컴퓨팅 인프라 계약에 따른 재무적 의무를 공개했다.

SEC 공시에 따르면 앤트로픽의 2026년 3분기 매출은 169억5600만달러로, 직전 분기 115억5500만달러보다 약 46.7% 증가했다. 지난해 같은 기간 매출 13억8200만달러와 비교하면 약 12.3배 규모다.

올해 1월부터 9월까지 누적 매출은 332억4200만달러로, 지난해 같은 기간 25억4500만달러보다 약 1206% 증가했다. 생성형 AI와 에이전틱 AI(Agentic AI)에 대한 기업 수요가 빠르게 확대되면서 앤트로픽의 매출 성장 속도도 가팔라진 것으로 나타났다.

그러나 매출 증가와 함께 AI 컴퓨팅 비용도 빠르게 늘었다. 3분기 컴퓨팅 및 인프라 비용은 98억6300만달러로, 직전 분기 55억5800만달러보다 약 77.5% 증가했다. 이는 해당 분기 매출의 약 58.2%에 해당하는 규모다.

3분기 영업손실은 5억6700만달러를 기록했다. 직전 분기에는 9억7400만달러의 영업이익을 기록했으나 다시 적자로 전환했다. AI 서비스 수요가 늘어나는 동시에 컴퓨팅 인프라와 사업 운영에 투입되는 비용도 확대되고 있음을 보여준다.

AI 컴퓨팅·인프라 지출 약정 8954억달러, 2030년까지 절반 집행 예상

이번 공시에서 가장 주목되는 부분은 앤트로픽이 공개한 장기 컴퓨팅 및 인프라 관련 지출 약정이다. 앤트로픽은 2026년 9월 30일 기준 및 그 이후 체결한 구매 약정과 리스계약 등을 포함해 총 약 8954억달러의 계약상 지출 의무가 있다고 밝혔다. 이 가운데 대부분은 AI 모델의 학습과 추론에 필요한 컴퓨팅 자원 및 인프라와 관련돼 있다.

전체 약정 가운데 약 4475억달러는 2030년 12월 31일까지 발생할 것으로 예상된다. 나머지 대부분은 2031년부터 2045년 사이에 발생하며, 약 698억달러는 2026년 9월 30일 이후 12개월 이내에 지급기일이 도래한다.

이는 이미 집행된 투자액이나 현재까지 발생한 비용이 아니라 향후 계약 조건에 따라 부담해야 할 지출 약정이다. 따라서 8954억달러 전체를 즉시 필요한 투자금이나 확정된 현금 지출액으로 해석해서는 안 된다.

특히 전체 약정 가운데 약 2138억달러는 계약 해지권이나 특정 조건 충족 여부에 영향을 받는 계약과 관련돼 있다. 일부 계약은 상대방의 자금 조달, 시설 확보, 규제 승인 등의 조건이 충족되지 않으면 종료될 수 있다.

앤트로픽은 장기 컴퓨팅 계약을 통해 AI 모델 개발과 서비스 제공에 필요한 연산 자원을 확보하고 있지만, 이러한 계약에는 실제 자원 사용량과 관계없이 일정 금액을 지급해야 하는 최소 구매 의무 등이 포함될 수 있다고 설명했다.

이는 AI 수요가 예상보다 빠르게 증가하면 연산 자원 부족이 발생할 수 있고, 반대로 수요가 기대에 미치지 못하면 확보한 인프라의 활용률이 낮아져 고정비 부담이 커질 수 있다는 의미다. 회사는 이러한 장기 투자에 필요한 자금을 영업활동에서 창출하는 매출과 외부 자본 조달을 통해 확보할 계획이다.

연간 10만달러 이상 고객 1만1900곳 돌파, 기업 AI 시장 확대

대규모 인프라 투자를 뒷받침하는 핵심 성장 동력은 기업 고객 증가다. 앤트로픽은 2026년 9월 말 기준 최근 12개월 동안 10만달러 이상의 매출을 발생시킨 고객이 1만1900곳을 넘어섰다고 밝혔다. 지난해 같은 시점의 950곳 이상과 비교하면 고객 기반이 1년 만에 12배 이상 확대된 셈이다.

연간 100만달러 이상의 매출을 발생시킨 고객도 1900곳을 넘어섰으며, 1000만달러 이상 고객은 약 250곳에 달했다. 이는 AI 서비스가 개별 부서의 시험적 도입을 넘어 기업의 주요 업무에 활용되는 사례가 증가하고 있음을 보여준다.

특히 연간 10만달러 이상 매출 고객 가운데 50% 이상은 2026년 3분기에 클로드 플랫폼(Claude Platform)과 앤트로픽의 자체 애플리케이션을 함께 사용한 것으로 나타났다. 지난해 4분기 약 30%에서 크게 높아진 수치다.

기업들이 AI 모델의 응용프로그램 인터페이스(API)를 활용하는 동시에 클로드 기반 업무 도구를 직접 사용하는 방식으로 활용 범위를 확대하고 있다는 의미다. 앤트로픽은 AI 코딩 도구 ‘클로드 코드(Claude Code)’를 비롯한 에이전틱 AI 제품의 확산도 기업 고객의 사용량 증가에 기여하고 있다고 설명했다.

AWS·구글·엔비디아·AMD 활용, 컴퓨팅 공급망 다변화

앤트로픽은 대규모 컴퓨팅 수요를 충족하기 위해 여러 반도체와 클라우드 인프라를 함께 활용하는 전략을 추진하고 있다. 공시에 따르면 회사는 아마존웹서비스(AWS)의 트레이니엄(Trainium), 구글의 텐서처리장치(TPU), 엔비디아(NVIDIA) 및 AMD의 그래픽처리장치(GPU)를 활용하는 다중 칩 컴퓨팅 구조를 운영하고 있다.

특정 반도체나 클라우드 사업자에 대한 의존도를 줄이면서 AI 모델의 학습과 추론에 필요한 자원을 비용과 성능에 따라 배분하는 방식이다.

앤트로픽은 자체적으로 데이터센터 용량을 확보하고 컴퓨팅 인프라를 구축하는 ‘앤트로픽 다이렉트(Anthropic Direct)’ 전략도 확대하고 있다. 데이터센터 공간과 전력 용량을 먼저 확보한 뒤 실제 컴퓨팅 수요에 맞춰 가속기 투자를 진행해 자본 투입 시점을 조정하려는 것이다.

이 같은 전략은 AI 모델 개발 경쟁에서 컴퓨팅 자원 확보가 중요한 경쟁 요소로 부상하고 있음을 보여준다. 동시에 장기 계약을 통해 확보한 인프라가 실제 매출과 현금흐름으로 얼마나 연결되는지가 향후 재무성과를 좌우할 것으로 예상된다.

나스닥 상장 추진, 공모가격·주식 수는 아직 미정

앤트로픽은 이번 수정 등록신고서를 통해 기업공개 절차도 이어가고 있다. 회사는 미국 나스닥 글로벌 셀렉트 마켓(Nasdaq Global Select Market)에 ‘ANT’라는 종목 기호로 상장을 신청했다. 다만 공모 주식 수와 공모가격 범위는 아직 확정되지 않았다.

이번 신고서는 상장을 위한 예비 투자설명서에 해당하며, SEC의 등록신고서 효력 발생 전에는 공모 주식을 판매할 수 없다. 앤트로픽은 델라웨어주 공익법인(Public Benefit Corporation) 구조를 채택하고 있다. AI 안전성과 인류의 장기적 이익을 고려한다는 기업 목적을 유지하면서 기업공개를 추진하는 것이 특징이다.

상장 이후에도 창업자와 장기적 공익 목적을 감독하는 별도의 지배구조를 통해 경영권과 AI 개발 방향에 대한 통제체계를 유지할 계획이다.

이번 공시는 프런티어 AI 기업의 성장과 비용 구조를 동시에 보여주는 중요한 사례다. 앤트로픽은 1년 만에 분기 매출을 12배 이상 확대하고 고액 기업 고객을 빠르게 확보했다. 생성형 AI가 기업의 실제 업무에 도입되면서 상당한 매출을 창출하는 산업으로 성장하고 있다는 점이 확인됐다.

반면 이러한 성장을 유지하기 위해서는 대규모 컴퓨팅 자원을 지속적으로 확보해야 한다. 약 8954억달러에 이르는 계약상 지출 약정은 AI 기업의 경쟁력이 모델 성능과 고객 확보뿐 아니라 장기적인 자본 조달 능력과 인프라 운영 효율에 의해서도 결정된다는 점을 보여준다.

특히 3분기 컴퓨팅 및 인프라 비용이 매출의 약 58%에 달하고 영업손실이 발생했다는 점은 향후 수익성 개선의 중요성을 부각한다. AI 기업이 확보한 컴퓨팅 자원을 실제 매출로 얼마나 효율적으로 전환하는지, 인프라 지출 증가 속도보다 매출과 현금흐름을 더 빠르게 늘릴 수 있는지가 중요한 평가 기준이 될 전망이다.

앤트로픽의 기업공개는 이러한 성장성과 비용 부담을 공개 자본시장에서 평가받는 계기가 될 것으로 보인다. AI 산업의 경쟁이 기술 개발과 시장점유율 확대를 넘어 수익성과 투자 지속가능성을 입증해야 하는 단계로 이동하고 있음을 보여준다.
articles.summary: 제공된 보도에 따르면 앤트로픽은 수정 IPO 등록신고서에서 약 8,954억달러의 장기 컴퓨팅·인프라 관련 계약상 지출 약정을 공개했다. 2026년 3분기 매출은 169억5,600만달러로 전년 동기의 약 12.3배였지만, 컴퓨팅·인프라 비용은 98억6,300만달러로 매출의 58.2%에 달했고 영업손실은 5억6,700만달러였다. 전체 약정 중 약 4,475억달러는 2030년 말까지 발생할 것으로 예상되며, 일부 계약은 해지권이나 선행 조건의 영향을 받는다. 이미 집행된 투자액과 미래 약정을 구분해야 하며, 기업 AI 수요 확대가 수익성 개선으로 곧바로 이어지지는 않는다는 점을 보여준다.

November 2, 2026

We’re planning our next internal security sprint at OpenAI, bringing new researchers and security partners together with our own teams to use our models to test and strengthen our systems. We’re partnering with Cathedral, whose researchers will use OpenAI’s models alongside our teams to challenge our defenses, bringing differentiated expertise and approaches to finding weaknesses and helping us protect our platforms.

We’re alsomaking improvementsto ourSecurity Bug Bounty programincluding more than quadrupling our rewards for critical findings. We want researchers to challenge our assumptions and help strengthen both our systems and the methods we use to defend them.

This is part of our ongoing effort to use AI to continuously find and fix weaknesses in our systems. Our last sprint showed what this approach can deliver. We dedicated 25% of our product engineers to finding and fixing weaknesses in our systems. Using Codex, engineers investigated findings, reproduced vulnerabilities in isolated environments and prepared patches for review.

We’re building on that work because traditional cyber defenses alone are no longer sufficient. Recent incidents across the industry show how quickly threats can emerge and how important it is to build continuous defensive loops to find and fix weaknesses before attackers do.

Keeping thedefender’s windowopen requires organizations to use frontier cyber capabilities to harden their systems. We’re using our most capable models to strengthen our own defenses and making them available toDaybreakcustomers. We’ve committed$1 billionin subsidized access over six months for frontline defenders protecting essential services and digital infrastructure. We’re also sharing ourarchitecture and lessons⁠from the last sprint, alongside ourblueprintfor empowering cyber defenders across industry and government.

We’ll keep advancing our models, using them to strengthen our own systems, and expanding access for trusted defenders. Keeping the defender’s window open will take action across the industry, and that work needs to start now.

articles.title: Mage-VL-Cowork: A Full Training Recipe to Learn Hybrid Computer Use From Evolved Harnesses
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.40747v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Effective computer-use agents (CUAs) should seamlessly combine visual GUI interaction with code and terminal execution within a single policy. We present Mage-VL-Cowork, a 4B hybrid CUA trained from a general multimodally aligned checkpoint through an end-to-end, progressive five-stage curriculum across midtraining, SFT, and RL. To power this curriculum at scale, Mage-CUA-Forge replaces per-task agent construction with reusable, skill-conditioned generation workflows and application-specific preparers, synthesizing 293,806 desktop and web tasks across 6,915 skills while reducing recurring per-task expenditure by 82.6%. Rather than directly distilling a default teacher, we evolve the teacher harness and instantiate specialized CUA harnesses to yield high-quality trajectories alongside stage-specific supervision. Mage-VL-Cowork-4B finally climbs to 66.0% on OSWorld-Verified through different training stages with more efficient reasoning cost, achieving state-of-the-art performance at its parameter size and pushing forward the frontier of on-device intelligence.
articles.summary: Mage-VL-Cowork는 시각적 GUI 조작과 코드·터미널 실행을 하나의 정책에 결합한 4B 컴퓨터 사용 에이전트 연구다. 중간학습·지도 미세조정·강화학습을 잇는 5단계 교육과정과 개선된 교사 하네스를 활용했으며, 데이터 생성 체계는 6,915개 기술에 걸쳐 293,806개 작업을 합성했다. 연구진은 반복적인 작업당 생성 비용을 82.6% 줄이고 OSWorld-Verified에서 66.0%를 달성했다고 보고했다. 소형 모델의 복합 업무 자동화 가능성을 보여주지만, 해당 결과만으로 실제 기기에서의 지연이나 운영 안정성까지 입증된 것은 아니다.

November 2, 2026

Launching a national program to help our future compute campuses support reliable, affordable electricity.

Today we’re launching theGrid Protectors Program, a national effort to support affordable, reliable electricity for families and businesses in the communities where we build. Working with utilities, regulators and policymakers, we’ll develop arrangements for our future campuses to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.

Whether it’s heating homes during a northern cold snap or running air conditioning through a southern heat wave, families need reliable electricity. Our goal is to make campus flexibility a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.

With U.S. data center capacity projected to exceed100 gigawatts by 2030⁠(opens in a new window), we have a once-in-a-generation opportunity to strengthen the electric grid by building campuses that can adjust their power use when communities need it most.

Through Grid Protectors, our ambition is to make this kind of flexibility a core part of how we build and operate future campuses. That means designing facilities to reduce electricity use when needed and working with utilities to agree on how much demand can be reduced, how quickly and for how long. The arrangements will differ by location, and we will share additional commitments as they are finalized.

Depending on local needs and the equipment available, we will also work with grid operators to supply power from on-site generation or storage, and use batteries and power controls to smooth changes in demand.

Power lines, substations and other grid infrastructure builds are a fixed cost whether demand is low or high. By using more electricity when the grid has room and reducing our use when it is under strain, we can help pay for that infrastructure while limiting the need for costly upgrades to meet peak demand. That can help keep costs down for other customers.

America needs more electricity to support economic growth, and AI is becoming a significant part of that demand. Families and small businesses should not be asked to subsidize a compute campus’s electricity needs. We’ve always been committed to paying our own energy costs, including the electricity we use and the infrastructure needed to serve our campuses. Large computing facilities should pay their costs and help utilities manage the systems they depend on.

For our planned Effingham County campus, we have committed to pay the full infrastructure and electric-service costs required to serve the project. Once the campus is operating, we can reduce the power we draw during times of need, helping preserve electricity for other customers.

Ouragreement with Georgia Power also includes⁠(opens in a new window)up to 1,000 megawatts of flexible demand response, freeing up power to help keep air conditioning running in hundreds of thousands of homes during extreme heat. For scale, that is equivalent to the average electricity demand of roughly 700,000 households. That’s more households than Washington, D.C., and Boston combined.

These compute facilities are much different than data centers built even a few years ago, allowing us to be flexible in our power demand.

This means we can turn down our demand so that families, small businesses, and other ratepayers will continue to have power. Building grid assets is expensive and Georgia Power says this flexibility can reduce the amount of new generation it needs to build to serve future growth. Although the campus is still in development, we intend for Effingham to serve as a pilot for Grid Protectors, building on an agreement that already provides a model for future campuses.

Imagine a restaurant in a vacation town. It needs enough tables and kitchen space for the busy season, but it has to pay for that capacity year-round. Regular customers help keep it in use and cover the bills when tourism slows. We are proposing to be that regular customer.

Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times. Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest. We still need to pay the costs our campuses create; the goal is for other customers to benefit, too.

Our agreement also contributes to Georgia Power’s broader plan to lower costs for customers. The utilityprojects approximately $950 million in annual customer savings beginning in 2029⁠(opens in a new window)from its portfolio of large-load agreements and expected growth, including Project Camellia. It estimates a benefit of at least $15 a month for a typical residential customer using 1,000 kilowatt-hours.

The Georgia agreement is a starting point. At OpenAI, through our Grid Protectors program, we see an opportunity to help communities keep the lights on even in times of emergency and high demand. We will work with utilities, regulators and policymakers to develop practical arrangements for the campuses we build in the future-arrangements that reflect local grid needs, help campuses support the grid when it is under pressure, and pay the costs we create. Long-term contracts and financial assurances can protect other customers if a project is delayed, reduced or canceled.

Flexibility cannot replace investment in new energy supply and transmission. Alongside those investments, our Grid Protectors program can help make the grid more reliable and protect families and small businesses from bearing the costs of AI infrastructure. That is the standard we want our compute campuses to meet.

articles.title: Zyphra AI Introduces Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA): A Path to True Subquadratic Attention
articles.content: Zyphra has released Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA), a sparse attention method built around a tree-structured indexer. ZHA targets a known gap in sparse attention: the indexer that picks tokens still scans the whole context. Zyphra’s technical paper shows ZHA can be distilled into frozen pretrained models with about 4B tokens. On Qwen3.6-35B-A3B it stays close to dense attention on reasoning, agentic coding and 256K retrieval benchmarks. TL;DR Size: It is a method that adds 81,920 trainable parameters to Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (about 0.00024%). Tested up to 256K context. Runs on: Retrofits frozen pretrained models after a 4B-token KL warmup at 32K context. Speedups come from a modeled H100 BF16 roofline. No optimized kernels released. An FP4 router variant was also tested. Performance: Within a few points of dense attention on 7 reasoning, coding and retrieval benchmarks. Best: LongBench v2 hits 63.4% (deep tree) vs 58.0% dense, using about 1.1% of keys. Worst: On NoPE-based Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, deep-tree RULER-13 drops 25.3 points below dense. What is Zyphra Hierarchical Attention (ZHA)? ZHA is a sparse attention method from Zyphra that finds relevant keys by searching a tree. It keeps the full KV cache. The tree only decides which cached keys each query reads. Fixed-state methods like SSMs and sliding windows saturate at long contexts. Fine-grained sparse methods like DeepSeek Sparse Attention score every past token with an indexer. The final attention is sparse, but the indexer still grows with the full context. Near 1M tokens, cited work shows indexing takes 60 to 90% of layer time. ZHA makes the search itself sparse. How does ZHA’s tree indexer work? Building the tree ZHA splits keys into contiguous chunks and compresses each chunk into a summary key. Summaries are grouped and compressed again, level by level. With chunk size 4, 6 levels cover 4,096 tokens per top node. Summaries come from a small set of learned reference queries. Each reference query gives a tangent-plane estimate of a chunk’s log attention mass. The max over these planes approximates how much attention any future query would give the chunk. How does top-p routing pick tokens? At decode time, a query scores the top-level nodes. It keeps the smallest set holding a fraction p of estimated attention mass. It then expands only those children, repeating until it reaches raw KV entries. Top-p makes the budget adaptive. A single-fact lookup touches few branches. A query that needs many scattered facts expands more. The first token is always kept as an attention sink. How does ZHA perform against dense attention and MSA? Zyphra team converted Qwen3.6-35B-A3B with 2 trees: deep (chunk 4, 6 levels) and wide (chunk 256, 1 level). Both use 16 reference queries and p = 0.95. It also trained a MiniMax Sparse Attention (MSA) indexer on 40B tokens, 10x ZHA’s budget. Across 28 tree geometries, RULER accuracy held steady when attending to 10 to 30% of keys. At fixed compression, deeper trees kept accuracy at higher sparsity. articles.title: NVIDIA Releases Auto Ontology: An Open Semantic Layer That Grounds AI Agent SQL
articles.content: NVIDIA has released Auto Ontology, an open library under the Apache 2.0 license. NVIDIA Auto Ontology is a semantic layer framework that builds a context layer from enterprise metadata. Agents use that layer to write SQL against certified business definitions. The repository states the problem plainly: a fast revenue answer is worthless if the number is wrong. TL;DR Library: Default LLM is nvidia/nemotron-3-nano-30b-a3b, with Nemotron embedding and reranking models. Runs on: Docker Compose for a local stack, or Kubernetes via Helm. Inference uses hosted NVIDIA NIM endpoints or self-hosted NIMs. Performance: Strong engineering, thin public evidence. Best: Ontology creation time cut by 90% in NVIDIA testing (self-reported). Worst: 0 published text-to-SQL accuracy scores. The eval repo ships a harness, not results. Bottom line: An open, MCP-ready context layer that any agent harness can query. But you must run the benchmarks yourself to trust it. What is NVIDIA Auto Ontology? It is a context layer that sits between an agent and the data warehouse. It tells the agent where data lives and what fields mean. It also says whether to use a field, how to use it, and where it came from. Here are the five jobs: Discover: generate ontologies from metadata and connect existing semantic models. Ground: give agents trusted meaning for metrics, entities and relationships. Validate: check generated queries against certified definitions and lineage. Expose: serve context through MCP, CLI and API. Learn: fold certified corrections back into the ontology. NVIDIA’s developer page frames the output as a starting ontology. Business experts still test, refine and certify it. How does Auto Ontology work? The stack has 4 core services. A Next.js 16 frontend handles the web UI and authentication on port 3000. A FastAPI backend with LangChain runs chat, NL-to-SQL and catalog APIs on port 3001. An ingestion worker writes embeddings on port 3002. Postgres with pgvector stores the catalog, the ontology and the vectors. Source databases can be Databricks, Postgres, Snowflake or DuckDB. Models are set through environment “triplets” of endpoint, key and model. Separate roles exist for reasoning, non-reasoning, embedding and reranking. Any OpenAI-compatible endpoint works. && What does the MCP server expose? The MCP server docs describe 9 read-only tools. ask_question returns the answer, the SQL and the rows as separate fields. Results cap at 100 rows. check_readiness confirms a compiled semantic layer and a live database connection exist. There is no tool for browsing raw schemas. NVIDIA chose that on purpose, so agents reach data through the semantic layer. The underlying OpenAPI spec publishes 87 operations. Sign-in runs through OAuth, and every call carries the signed-in user’s permissions. How is it benchmarked? NVIDIA ships a separate harness, auto-ontology-eval. It runs 2 arms in NeMo Gym: a schema-only LLM control and the ontology-grounded agent. Scoring is deterministic execution match, with no LLM judge. Bundled datasets include BIRD Dev (1,534 questions, 11 databases) and Mini-Dev (500 questions). FDABench-Lite adds 169 questions, and BEAVER defaults to a 100-question sample. The harness repo adds 2 limitations. Optional few-shot exemplars and value anchors go to the ontology arm only. A delta measured with them covers those inputs, not grounding alone. Its tested configuration also routes both arms through a Claude model on NVIDIA’s inference gateway. How does it compare with other semantic layers? Kubernetes users get a Helm chart and a DEPLOYMENT.md guide. NVIDIA team also publishes the backend as an NGC container. An NVIDIA API key from build.nvidia.com covers the default models. Key Takeaways Auto Ontology generates a starting semantic layer from enterprise metadata. Agents query it through 9 read-only MCP tools, plus CLI and API. NVIDIA reports 90% faster ontology creation in its own testing. No text-to-SQL accuracy scores are published yet. Defaults to Nemotron on NIM, but accepts any OpenAI-compatible endpoint. Measuring AI progress on the tasks that matter in everyday life.

OpenAI’s mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits all of humanity. For the more than one billion people who currently use ChatGPT every week, we want to build AI that can help with the practical challenges of everyday life, like finding childcare, accessing government services, creating a budget, preparing for school, modifying recipes, ordering groceries, designing workout plans, and more.

When someone is looking for help making their life easier, they need more than advice or a chat response. To be a truly helpful personal assistant, ChatGPT should be able to take actions that actually get things done.

To measure model performance over time on everyday tasks, we built an evaluation of tasks covering areas where users wanted the most help from AI and personal agents. We used this evaluation to track and drive improvement in model performance on everyday tasks over the past year.

To identify the tasks people value most, we started with two large studies that track how people spend time in both the U.S. and internationally: theAmerican Time Use Survey⁠(opens in a new window)and theMultinational Time Use Study⁠(opens in a new window). Together, these datasets provide a detailed catalog of everyday life tasks that people do across different demographics, times of day, and seasons. To understand where people would most value AI assistance, we expanded on these existing surveys with a new demographically representative survey of 3,995 respondents. For each task, we asked a variety of questions to identify the areas where everyday people most wanted help from a personal assistant. The resulting tasks span the most important areas that people want help with, including caregiving, health, education, household administration, personal finances, shopping, and accessing government services.

Below are some examples of how our current models perform on practical workflows from everyday life.

Compare kindergartens near our new home and shortlist the best fits.

I’ve narrowed it to three kindergartens and organized the enrollment details. Two preferences still need your call. Want to review the shortlist?

Help me organize our community’s flood preparation volunteer force for four neighbors needing floodproofing assistance.

I’ve prepared a simple action plan to help volunteers assess the sites mentioned and help them prepare for upcoming severe weather.

Find a home in Luzerne County that fits my budget, has a separate living unit, and keeps my commute short after school drop-off. Add the deed to my cart so I can review it.

I found one home that meets your requirements. I’ve calculated the transfer tax and added the deed to your country records cart to review.

Set up an easy way for grandma and me to watch the game together remotely.

The easiest watch setup is ready, with a backup if the stream fails. Want me to walk you through it with grandma?

Help my parent adjust to a new diabetes diagnosis with a practical care and meal plan.

The first-week plan is ready, including meals, reminders, and questions for the care team. Want to review it together before you share it with your parent?

Our latest models score very highly on many LifeVal tasks.See more

Over the past year, we’ve trained our models to become much faster, more capable, and more aligned on browser use, computer use, and connectors tasks. Enabling these capabilities in ChatGPT also expands the types of tasks the model can help with, helping move ChatGPT beyond a chat tool and towards a truly agentic personal assistant.

To ensure AGI benefits all of humanity, we need to measure and improve model progress on what matters in the lives of everyday people. That means going beyond academic assessments of model knowledge and actually measuring how well AI models can help people navigate decisions, manage everyday responsibilities, and get meaningful things done. We are hopeful that LifeVal represents a step towards that goal.

articles.title: Can Personal Requirements Become Supervision for Planning?
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.40992v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Managing multiple chronic conditions through diet requires satisfying disease- and medication-specific requirements jointly across meals and days while preserving established eating habits. These requirements are public in clinical guidelines and drug labels, yet turning them into a feasible plan for one person remains difficult for language-model agents. In our dietitian-approved weekly planning evaluation built from NHANES, thirteen models, from medically fine-tuned 8B models to GPT-6.1 Sol, pass fewer than 3% of complete plans through direct generation. Explicit rules, higher reasoning effort, or model-directed tools leave GPT-6.1 Sol at no more than 8%. We present Noura, which pairs LLM planning with executable personal specifications instantiated from public clinical guidance and individual health and dietary profiles. During planning, the specification grounds foods, optimizes portions, checks the complete multi-day plan, and guides revision. Our key insight is that a specification that rejects a plan can also determine what to learn from it. Noura turns executed plans and contextually credited revisions into supervision for compact models, recovering targets even from trajectories that never achieve complete success. The same specification supplies supervised targets, preferences, and rewards for post-training. On 4,993 held-out participants, Noura-SFT raises Qwen3-14B's complete-plan pass rate from 24.0% to 72.5% within the same execution loop, cuts rule violations by 97.5% with no observed critical failures, and improves dietary quality. The locally hosted 14B planner incurs fewer rule violations than its GPT-6 Luna teacher. A matched comparison shows that executed targets reduce rule violations by 41% over model-written proposals. Across four Qwen, Phi, and Llama backbones, self-training alone reduces rule violations by 41-61% on a 1,249-person population subset.
articles.summary: Noura는 여러 만성질환과 약물·식습관 제약을 함께 만족하는 주간 식단을 만들기 위해 LLM 계획과 실행 가능한 개인별 명세를 결합한 연구다. 명세가 식품과 분량을 검증·최적화하고 계획 수정 과정을 학습 신호로 전환해, 같은 실행 루프 안에서 Qwen3-14B의 전체 계획 통과율을 24.0%에서 72.5%로 높였다. 별도 평가 참가자 4,993명에서 규칙 위반은 97.5% 감소했고 관찰된 치명적 실패는 없었다고 보고했다. 의료 지침을 검증 가능한 제약과 후학습 신호로 연결한 점이 중요하지만, 이는 식단 계획 평가 결과이며 임상적 효과나 실제 사용의 안전성을 확정하지 않는다.

articles.title: In-Model Context Compression with Agentic Soft Tokens for Long-Horizon LLM Agents
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.41291v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Long-horizon LLM agents play an important role in solving complex and sustained tasks, with ever-growing interaction contexts. However, these accumulated contexts will raise substantial computational cost and obscure key decision-relevant evidence. Existing methods typically train external compressors or context-management agents to rewrite context as shorter hard-token sequences, but such external selection may not align with the LLM's evolving representation and is necessarily lossy. In this paper, we introduce Agentic Soft-Token Compression (ASTC), a training-free compression method using soft tokens within LLM agent for long-horizon tasks. Specifically, ASTC uses the model's native recurrent dynamics to determine the already absorbed information, leveraging the commonly-used hybrid Gated Delta Network (GDN)-attention. It then carries this information forward as agentic soft tokens while retaining exact values as hard tokens. The resulting compact sequence reduces later-layer computation and yields reusable KV caches, extending the savings across the agent's trajectory. Extensive experiments on long-horizon tasks show that ASTC matches or exceeds the uncompressed agent's accuracy with up to 50.68% fewer end-to-end Attention Pairs, while trained compressors require 15.4 to 103.7 times more Attention Pairs per successful task. These findings highlight agentic soft tokens as a model-native way to carry absorbed context forward as the task representation evolves.
articles.summary: Agentic Soft-Token Compression은 장기 작업 에이전트의 누적 문맥을 외부 요약기 없이 모델 내부 소프트 토큰으로 압축하는 학습 불필요 방식이다. Gated Delta Network와 어텐션을 결합한 구조의 순환 상태를 이용해 이미 흡수한 정보를 전달하고, 정확한 값은 하드 토큰으로 남기며 KV 캐시도 재사용한다. 연구진은 비압축 에이전트와 동등하거나 더 높은 정확도를 유지하면서 종단 간 Attention Pairs를 최대 50.68% 줄였다고 보고했다. 다만 이 지표는 실제 실행 시간과 동일하지 않으며, 적용 가능성은 해당 하이브리드 구조를 전제로 판단해야 한다.

articles.title: Opening the Box Changes the Cat: LLMs Detect Chain-of-Thought Monitoring - What now?
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.40946v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning allows large language models (LLMs) to generate intermediate reasoning traces in natural language while solving complex tasks. These traces can support safety monitoring by exposing potentially harmful plans before actions are executed. In this work, we investigate the conditions under which LLMs infer the presence of CoT monitoring from direct and indirect environmental cues and examine how this inference affects their subsequent behavior. Our observations suggest that oversight is an interactive process: while a monitor inspects a model's reasoning, traces left by monitoring interventions can allow the model to infer that its thoughts are being observed and to adapt its behavior accordingly. We show that even subtle environmental cues, such as timing-related signals from timeouts and operation durations, can reveal the presence of monitoring and trigger models to adapt their behavior. Across repeated episodes and interaction loops, we further observe that models can form statistical estimates of the monitor's effectiveness and use these estimates to guide attempts to evade detection. These findings highlight the need to evaluate CoT-based oversight under adaptive conditions, where the monitoring process itself may influence the behavior it seeks to observe.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 LLM이 타임아웃이나 작업 소요 시간 같은 간접적인 환경 신호를 통해 추론 과정 감시의 존재를 알아차리고 행동을 바꿀 수 있다고 보고했다. 반복 상호작용에서는 감시의 효과를 통계적으로 추정하고 이를 탐지 회피 시도에 활용하는 행동도 관찰했다. 이는 추론 기록을 수동적으로 읽는 것만으로 감독을 평가하기 어렵고, 감시 개입 자체가 모델에 노출되는 적응적 상황을 시험해야 한다는 의미다. 제공된 초록에는 모델별 발생률이나 세부 실험 조건이 없어 모든 모델에 일반화할 수는 없다.

articles.title: Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.41040v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: LLM agents serve natural-language requests through tools, data sources, and other agents, and even simple requests often need several interdependent calls. Typically, the LLM picks these calls by trial and error, with no guarantee of an executable plan. We present Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning (CGAP), which instead reasons about what a request requires and what tools provide. CGAP compiles the tool catalog deterministically into a PDDL model, uses an LLM to turn the request into goals, and solves the model with a classical planner. Since tool outputs are unknown in advance, the model is abstract, tracking which inputs are available, not their values. During execution, an LLM adds entity-specific calls that abstract plans omit, and deterministic checks reject any that break the plan. Every argument is drawn from a cited source, such as a conversation span or an earlier tool response, and each requested result counts as delivered only after an LLM verifier checks it against the request. With three LLMs on ToolSandbox, ComplexFuncBench, BFCL multi-turn, and $\tau^2$-bench retail, CGAP outperforms a standard tool-calling agent by up to 28.9 points.
articles.summary: Capability-Grounded Agentic Planning은 도구 선택을 LLM의 시행착오에만 맡기지 않고 도구 목록을 PDDL 모델로 변환해 고전적 계획기로 실행 순서를 구한다. LLM은 사용자 요청을 목표로 바꾸고 실행 중 필요한 엔터티별 호출을 추가하며, 결정론적 검사가 계획 위반을 걸러내고 각 인수의 출처를 추적한다. 세 가지 LLM과 네 가지 도구 사용 벤치마크에서 표준 도구 호출 에이전트보다 최대 28.9%포인트 높은 성능을 보고했다. 업무 도구의 입출력 의존성과 결과 검증을 명시적으로 관리한다는 점이 유용하지만, 추상 계획이 도구 반환값 자체를 미리 보장하는 것은 아니다.

articles.title: On the Origin and Evolution of Training-Inference Mismatch in LLM Reinforcement Learning
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.40945v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: On-policy reinforcement learning for large language models assumes that training responses are sampled from the current policy. In practice, an inference engine samples the responses and a separate trainer computes the gradients, and the \textbf{training-inference mismatch} between the two makes the training data off-policy. The mismatch has two sources, the numerics of the engine and the stale weights of asynchronous sampling, and a correction that stabilizes training under one source can fail under the other. \textit{We ask which property of a mismatch source decides the correction it needs.} Evaluating the trainer at the sampler's weights splits each sampled-token error exactly into a \textit{numerical discrepancy} of the engine and a \textit{policy lag} of the trainer, and we follow both through training. The numerical discrepancy stays approximately constant, so it biases the updates by a nearly fixed amount, and centering the score at each prefix removes its leading bias. The policy lag is produced by the trainer's own updates: the bias it leaves enters the next update, which enlarges the next lag and closes a feedback loop. Importance weighting cuts this loop only while the lag ratio stays concentrated, and on Qwen3-1.7B it fails at the step where the effective sample size of the ratio falls below one half. From this account we derive the \textbf{discrepancy-lag correction} (DLC), which centers the numerical discrepancy, clips the lag ratio against the sampler's weights and resynchronizes the sampler when this effective sample size falls below one half. Under a stale sampler, DLC keeps the KL divergence from on-policy training within twice the KL between two independent on-policy trainings on Qwen3-0.6B and Qwen3-1.7B, and its resynchronization prevents collapses that the per-token corrections leave and that a KL measured on the sampler's prefixes does not detect.
articles.summary: 이 연구는 LLM 강화학습에서 샘플을 생성하는 추론 엔진과 학습기의 불일치를 수치 오차와 비동기 가중치 지연으로 분리했다. 수치 오차는 비교적 일정한 편향을 만들지만, 정책 지연은 업데이트가 다음 지연을 키우는 피드백 루프를 형성해 서로 다른 보정이 필요하다는 분석이다. 제안한 DLC는 수치 편향을 중심화하고 지연 비율을 클리핑하며, 유효 표본 크기가 절반 아래로 내려가면 샘플러를 재동기화한다. Qwen3-0.6B와 1.7B 실험에서는 정책 불일치를 억제하고 다른 토큰별 보정이 막지 못한 붕괴를 방지했지만, 더 큰 모델에서의 검증은 제시되지 않았다.

articles.title: EDU-Jev Training System-One Decision Models for Education
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.41079v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: Many automated decisions in education involve choosing from a fixed set of options: assigning a rubric score, checking whether an answer meets a marking criterion, or identifying the first wrong step in a solution. Generative language models are increasingly used to make these decisions, but their responses require parsing, longer outputs increase inference costs, and confidence expressed in words does not necessarily reflect the probability of being correct. We present EDU-Jev, a family of single-pass ("System One") decision models at 0.8B, 2B and 4B parameters. Given an assessment context and a question with predefined answer options, the model returns a probability distribution over those options without generating text. A pointer head scores a marker for each option, ensuring the predictions are restricted to the allowed choices. Training uses a single supervised stage with soft cross-entropy against the available target label distributions; calibration is assessed empirically. Across twelve education benchmarks, EDU-Jev 4B achieves an average accuracy of 67.6%, exceeding the strongest of five commercial decision APIs by 9.4 percentage points and the best open 4B decision model by 18.7 points. On four cross-domain education sets, it matches the strongest API, which remains ahead on general decision-making and reasoning tasks. The 2B model processes about 150 decisions per second on a single H100 GPU.
articles.summary: EDU-Jev는 교육 평가에서 미리 정한 선택지의 확률 분포를 한 번의 순전파로 출력하는 0.8B·2B·4B 결정 모델 계열이다. 포인터 헤드로 허용된 선택지만 점수화해 생성 텍스트의 파싱을 없애고, 목표 라벨 분포에 대한 소프트 교차엔트로피로 학습한다. 연구진은 12개 교육 벤치마크에서 4B 모델이 평균 정확도 67.6%를 기록해 비교한 최상위 상용 결정 API보다 9.4%포인트 높았으며, 2B는 H100 한 대에서 초당 약 150건을 처리했다고 보고했다. 정형 채점의 비용과 처리량 측면에서 유망하지만, 일반 의사결정과 추론 과제에서는 상용 비교 API가 앞섰다.

articles.title: Automatic Construction of Strong Simple Baselines
articles.content:
arXiv:2610.40700v1 Announce Type: new 
Abstract: To rigorously establish the value of a novel deep learning method, it must be compared against appropriate baselines. As deep learning has become increasingly common in the physical and life sciences, there have been numerous cases in which apparent progress has turned out to be an artifact of omitted or missing baselines. In this work, we investigate whether this problem can be mitigated by using large language models to automate the construction of baselines. We assemble 36 supervised classification and regression tasks from peer-reviewed studies in Nature, Science, and Cell-family journals that investigate novel deep learning methods for scientific applications. We then use a language model to construct simple baselines for each task. These automatically constructed baselines are strong, recovering a median of 95.5% (mean 85.7%) of the gap between a trivial predictor and the score of the deep learning model. The median simple baseline matches or exceeds the performance of the deep learning model in 12 studies. We further examine the variation across scientific domains and publication venues and we characterize the effects of test-time compute and access to different levels of study context. As human peer review has struggled to keep up with the rapidly increasing volume of research articles in recent years, our results suggest that automated baseline construction is a practical and scalable check on deep learning contributions in the physical and life sciences.
articles.summary: 연구진은 Nature·Science·Cell 계열 학술지의 과학 분야 딥러닝 연구에서 36개 분류·회귀 과제를 모아 LLM으로 단순한 비교 기준 모델을 자동 구성했다. 생성된 기준 모델은 단순 예측기와 논문 속 딥러닝 모델 사이 성능 격차의 중앙값 기준 95.5%를 회복했고, 12개 연구에서는 기준 모델 성능 중앙값이 딥러닝 모델과 같거나 더 높았다. 복잡한 신규 기법의 기여를 판단하기 전에 강력한 단순 기준선을 확보해야 한다는 점을 정량적으로 보여준다. 연구 자동화의 실용적 용도를 새 모델 발명뿐 아니라 기존 성과의 재검증과 동료심사 지원으로 넓힌 결과다.
